newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: DOWNER TO ARRIVE IN KUALA LUMPUR THIS AFTERNOON

One of Foreign Minister Alexander Downer's first tasks at regional security talks in Malaysia this weekend is expected to involve explaining the accidental release of a South Pacific briefing document.

Malaysia, host of this year's ASEAN conference, drew some critical mentions in the secret Australian paper with references to Malaysian logging interests being involved in corruption in Papua New Guinea and Solomon Islands.
Mr Downer will need to navigate past the problem before confronting the continuing Malaysian veto on Australia taking part in the Asia-Europe summits.
In talks with the nine ASEAN Foreign Ministers, Mr Downer will stress Australia's view that it has strong claims to a seat to the summits, the second of which will be in London next March.
Canberra already acknowledges there will be no invitation for Australia to attend a separate Asian summit to be held in Malaysia in December.
Mr Downer is also expected to seek broad agreement on approaches to Burma and Cambodia when he arrives in Kuala Lumpur this afternoon.
He is planning to have individual meetings with the Foreign Ministers of Burma and Cambodia, which will be among the 21 countries attending the forum.
Australia believes the forum is Asia's most important security conference, and will press the forum to begin moving beyond dialogue and develop mechanisms to prevent conflict in Asia.
Despite criticism from China, Mr Downer will repeat Australia's view that the U.S. military presence is a stabilising presence in the region.
LANGE DOES NOT BELIEVE LEAKED PAPERS WILL DAMAGE RELATIONS
Former New Zealand Prime Minister, David Lange, believes the publication of sensitive documents critical of New Zealand is part of a calculated campaign by senior bureaucrats.
Trans-Tasman relations have been shaken by the documents which are critical of New Zealand Ministers, and of the country's reluctance to increase spending of defence.
Mr Lange has told ABC radio that while he did not believe the affair would seriously damage Australia--New Zealand relations, he levels the blame at Foreign Affairs officials in both countries.
Mr Lange says the incident could not be anything but a calculated act by an official within one of the bureaucracies.
But Mr Lange says official briefing papers containing unflattering descriptions of political figures are nothing new. Mr Lange says such documents are prepared for all Governments.
MOORA COMMUNITY HIT BY YET ANOTHER TRAGEDY
North of Perth, and detectives investigating the fatal shootings near Moora yesterday are still withholding the identity of the dead people.
But word has spread through the town, with residents shocked and saddened by yet another tragedy in the small farming community.
Within the past 15 months, they have lost six teenagers in an horrific traffic accident, and one of the Port Arthur massacre victims was also from Moora.
This morning, the townspeople are waking up to yet another shock.
The small wheat belt town of Moora is in mourning today following the shooting of a well-known farming family.
The couple, whose names have not yet been released, were shot by their young son in what police believe to be a double murder suicide.
The incident happened at the family's farmhouse, 16 kilometres south of Moora.
The father who was shot dead was known as an outgoing man. He was chair of the hospital board, a long-standing member of Apex and the Moora Rovers football club.
Police are still at the scene with relatives, trying to piece together yesterday's tragic shooting.
OPPOSITION SAYS FOREIGN AFFAIRS CUTS SEND BAD SIGNAL
The Federal Opposition claims the latest round of cuts to the Department of Foreign Affairs is taking jobs from Australians and giving them to foreigners.
Shadow Industrial Relations Minister, Bob McMullan, says the Government is sending the wrong signal to our overseas trading partners.
As many as 225 jobs nationwide will go under plans revealed yesterday by Departmental Secretary Phillip Flood, with at least 50 of those in Canberra.

Mr McMullan says with the Department proposing to use people living overseas to fill jobs currently occupied by Australians, the Government is putting this country's international reputation further at risk.

"It sends a very bad signal in three ways: one, more jobs gone in Canberra; two, at a very time when our international reputation is in tatters we are reducing our representation; and thirdly, what you're seeing is Australian jobs going, being replaced by ... people from other countries", Mr McMullan said.
NEGOTIATIONS PLANNED TO END BORAL DISPUTES
The timber workers union, the CFMEU, hopes negotiations this morning will put an end to industrial action at Boral timber mills in the south and central-west of New South Wales.
Boral's workers have this week been conducting ongoing industrial action.
Workers at Boral's Bathurst, Oberon and Tumbarumba mills have been on strike this week, claiming the company has brokered individual contracts while a collective agreement still exists.
The CFMEU's Andrew Harden says staff are committed to the strike.
Oberon and Tumbarumba set up picket lines yesterday to prevent management from unloading materials at the two mills.
But Oberon and Tumbarumba have now voted to return to work today, while Bathurst staff have vowed to continue the industrial action.
High level talks are being held this morning in Sydney, between the CFMEU and Boral management, in a bid to end the dispute.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
